text.p: Australian merchandise imports rose one percent in December, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Market forecasts for the data had centred on a flat result, and ranged from a two percent fall to a 3.1 percent rise.
The following is a selection of ecopnomists immediate reactions to the data.
JOHN KRYIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"If we take the December quarter as a whole, that shows that imports are probably up about two or three percent. That's pretty much in line with what we think is reasonably good growth at the moment and the rise in imports that we are seeing doesn't seem to equate with a picture of a flat economy that many people have been presenting. We think the current account is probably going to come in a little better than what we saw in November."

"It's come in pretty much in line with our expectations. I guess it shows some disquiet that there'll still be a higher current account deficit after November's A$1.9 billion, but we don't think so despite the fact that we thought that imports would rise. The reason for that is that we think there's going to be a nice bounce in exports. We're not concerned about the current account as a result of these numbers. Obviously, strong imports don't help the case for another cut in Reserve Bank interest rates, although in my view the main determinant of what happens with interest rates will be more on the inflation front."
SUSAN CREIGHTON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ABN AMRO:

"A little bit stronger than market expectations. It is interesting the break up of the imports. We would have expected a stronger figure for capital goods imports, but effectively it's wiped out the six percent gain that we got in November. However, overall we do think that capital goods imports will be the major driver of import growth over coming months. For the current account deficit ... I wouldn't be surprised to see another A$1.9/2.0 billion current account deficit."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The seasonally adjusted number has been edging higher for each of the last five months. While it's clearly volatile between capital, consumption and intermediate goods, it's still reasonably consistent with the economy doing something. It's probably consistent with an economy running a little below potential but a long long way from a hard landing. These are probably consistent with a current account deficit back towards A$1.6 billion."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"The figures are not terribly significant. A little surprising that imports of consumer goods are continuing to rise given other evidence of weakness in consumer spending. The decline in capital imports perhaps a little disappointing, although the relationship between imports and capital goods and business investment isn't close. But it looks as though we will have a current account deficit fairly close to A$2 billion unless there is a surprising rebound in exports."
